  • Recent findings suggest that “Our harvest being gotten in, our governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a special manner rejoice together after we had gathered the fruit of our labors.
  • Sources indicate that that sounds a little more like deer camp than grandma’s house.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, pumpkin pie, and football. In America, that’s usually what’s on the menu on the fourth Thursday in November. But in the fall of 1621, the original Thanksgiving meal didn’t resemble this in the slightest. The Pilgrims at Plymouth Plantation had a lot to be thankful for. The Wampanoag helped them survive the previous winter and harvest plenty of food over the summer. The two groups decided to come together and celebrate this for a few days with a feast, during which they ate a mix of wild fish and game. Here is an excerpt from one of two firsthand accounts from a man named Edward Winslow:.

Recent findings suggest that “Our harvest being gotten in, our governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a special manner rejoice together after we had gathered the fruit of our labors. They four in one day killed as much fowl as, with a little help beside, served the tech giant almost a week. At which time, amongst other recreations, we exercised our arms, many of the Indians coming amongst us, and among the rest their greatest king Massasoit, with some ninety men, whom for three days we entertained and feasted, and they went out and killed five deer, which they brought to the plantation and bestowed on our governor, and upon the captain and others.”.

Sources indicate that that sounds a little more like deer camp than grandma’s house. Along with a pile of venison and week’s supply of fowl, it’s not out of the question to assume there were also dried fruits, berries, nuts, fish, and shellfish at the feast. Being that most of these things are available to hunters and anglers, we took a deep dive into some of our favorite recipes. In the spirit of that original Thanksgiving meal, here are eight ways to bring back some wild game to the table this season.

Sources indicate that the Wampanoag showed the colonists a lot ways to grow and keep food, but neither group had access to refrigeration. Instead, things like berries and other fruit had to be eaten fresh or preserved. The most likely way they would have done this is by drying, but there’s another way to preserve fruit without refrigeration. Canning has been done for generations, and it’s still a perfect way to preserve wild berries for months. The pilgrims wouldn’t have had the sugar for this wild black raspberry jam recipe, but it still goes good with butter and toast, on a leftover turkey sandwich, or even some acorn-flour pancakes.

Industry observers note that today lobsters and other shellfish are considered delicacies, but 400 years ago, they were a staple. The Atlantic coastline provided Wampanoag and the colonists with clams, mussels, and lobster. But there’s also another crustacean, readily available in freshwater, that’s just as worthy of dipping in clarified butter: the crayfish. Here’s a classic crayfish etouffee to serve alongside the main course.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, melt the butter and add the flour. You are going to make a roux: over medium heat, stir the roux until it darkens to the color of peanut butter (about 20 minutes). Add the onions, celery, and green peppers, stirring to combine. Add the garlic, tomato paste, and Worcestershire. Stir for a couple of minutes. Pour in the stock and the cooked crayfish tail meat. Stir for a few minutes until the roux in well incorporated into the stock and it starts to boil. Turn the heat down to a simmer, and add the Cajun seasoning. Then simmer for about 20 minutes until the etouffee thickens. Serve over wild rice or plain white rice. If you like yours a little hotter, add Crystal hot sauce or your favorite hot sauce.

In the first sentence of the Winslow account, there’s a mention of fowl:.

“Our harvest being gotten in, our governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a special manner rejoice together after we had gathered the fruit of our labors.”.

Recent findings suggest that turkey is considered fowl, but the first thanksgiving probably included waterfowl instead. Ducks and geese would have been easier for the settlers and the Wampanoag to catch and cook. They are also more plentiful in the wild. The birds were most likely roasted over a fire. Spit roasting a whole bird is an involved process, and most will opt for an oven instead, given a chance. If you’re thinking about swapping duck for a turkey this year, this wild duck and squash curry is an excellent place to start.

Industry observers note that another bird readily available in the 17th century was the passenger pigeon. When populations were at their peak, it is said that flocks were so thick they would black out the sky. Unfortunately, this didn’t last. Due to heavy market hunting and habitat loss, the passenger pigeon is now extinct. A similar bird (though not closely related) is the mourning dove. In fact, one of the last living wild passenger pigeons was found roosting with mourning doves.

A classic popper recipe will work with doves and most other upland birds (and it also pairs well with football). But most dove hunters already have that recipe figured out. Instead, here’s a flaky cheese and pepper dove roll recipe that’s sure to please.

Fish played a substantial part in the colonist’s lives. They were loaned money to start the colony, and they planned to pay some of their debts back by fishing. Atlantic white cod would have been the fish of choice, though they would have also had access to other fish like runs Atlantic salmon. Here’s a linguini with salmon cream sauce recipe that makes use of the leftover, extra meat after filleting a fish.

Bring a large stock pot with salted water to a boil over high heat and cook your pasta according to the directions on the package. Reserve one cup of the pasta water before draining. Drain the noodles and set aside in a colander until ready to use.

In a large pan, melt the butter over medium heat, add the shallots and garlic, and cook until soft (about 2 minutes). Season with a pinch of salt, and black pepper to taste. Add the wine and cook until almost all the wine is evaporated. Add the heavy cream and the parmesan and stir together, cooking until the cream thickens up a bit (1-2 minutes). Add the pasta and toss with the cream sauce. If the sauce is too thick, add some of the pasta water until you get a creamy sauce. Toss in the parsley, and serve topped with grated parmesan. This will make six healthy servings.

Deer meat was likely the centerpiece of the first thanksgiving. After all, the Wampanoag brought five deer with them to the feast. Simple but effective, here’s the best way to apply heat to a backstrap and achieve perfection. And, just in case you have five deer on hand and a village to feed, here’s a guide on how to cook every scrap of meat on them.

According to recent reports, so where did this turkey thing come from anyway? The one other written account from the autumn of 1621 does mention that the pilgrims had turkey, although nobody is certain that it was eaten at the feast. The second account from William Bradford states:.

“And besides waterfowl there was great store of wild turkeys, of which they took many, besides venison, etc.”.

Long after Bradford’s death, his journal was found and reprinted in the 1850s, and for some reason, people really liked the part about turkey. During that time, Sarah Josepha Hale, the editor of a magazine called Godey’s Lady’s Book, promoted the turkey as a centerpiece of the table. Hale was also a strong voice behind Thanksgiving Day becoming a national holiday. She wrote letters and even petitioned a few presidents.

Recent findings suggest that finally, in 1863, Abraham Lincoln declared the day a national holiday, and turkey has been the star of the show ever since. Whether wild turkey was eaten during the first Thanksgiving or not, it’s still delicious. If you have a left-over gobbler from the spring, or one you’ve shot this fall, this wild take on a classic Thanksgiving turkey recipe is sure to get some attention at your table.

• 2 gallons water • 2 oranges • 2 lemons • 1 onion, cut into 8 pieces • 1 cup brown sugar • 1 cup Kosher salt • Couple sprigs of fresh thyme or rosemary.

Make brining mixture, mixing all ingredients. Squeeze the oranges and lemons into the mixture and toss in the rinds too. Soak turkey in a cooler with ice and the brining mixture overnight. If you need more brine, use ½ cup salt and ½ cup brown sugar for every gallon of water. Use additional fruit as desired.

I lightly stuff the turkey with a couple celery stalks, onion pieces and a couple carrots, along with a half lemon and half orange from the brine mixture.

1. Place the turkey breast side up on a rack in a shallow roasting pan. Do not add water.

2. Before placing the turkey in the oven, you may want to brush it with cooking oil, melted butter or margarine, although it’s not necessary.

3. Cover the turkey with a loose tent of heavy-duty aluminum foil to prevent over browning, allow for maximum heat circulation and keep the turkey moist. To make a tent, tear off a sheet of foil 5 to 10 inches longer than the turkey. Crease the foil crosswise through the center and place over the turkey, crimping loosely onto the sides of the pan to hold it in place.

4. Roast according to the below chart.

5. To brown the turkey, remove the foil tent 20 to 30 minutes before roasting is finished, and continue cooking until the meat thermometer reaches 185 F.

Recent findings suggest that the following times are based on an oven preheated to 325 F. Use shorter cooking times for wild turkey so it doesn’t dry out.

It Would’ve Been the Best Duck Hunt of Our Lives. Instead, We Almost Died

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the greatest ordeals of my life began on a bleak, heavily overcast day, with a strong north wind and temperatures never rising above 22°.
  • According to recent reports, the Floodway was still timberland.
  • Industry observers note that george was an able physician and loyal friend, but he could never become a hunter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the greatest ordeals of my life began on a bleak, heavily overcast day, with a strong north wind and temperatures never rising above 22°. Dr. George Dahnke and I, both of Memphis, had decided to hunt ducks in the Floodway over in Arkansas. We’d heard reports that mallards were swarming on Section 16 of the Floodway, and the ducks were there, as we were to learn the hard way.

According to recent reports, the Floodway was still timberland. About 100,000 acres of it had been dammed and canalized to prevent the St. Francis River from flooding the towns of Marked Tree and Parkin. The forest floor was flooded all year, hence, the lure for ducks.

Industry observers note that george was an able physician and loyal friend, but he could never become a hunter. Though he was an enthusiast who tried hard, he began hunting too late in life and was too dedicated to the practice of medicine to give much thought to hunting. Further, he was not physically fit, being too soft through lack of exercise.

Industry observers note that we drove to the Floodway with my father-in-law, Mr. Ambrose, who was past 70 years of age. He realized that he was not up to the effort involved in as much boating as George and I planned to do, so he arranged for a local guide to paddle his boat and keep him close to the clubhouse.

This story, “I’ll Never Hunt Ducks Again,” appeared in the March 1982 issue of Outdoor Life.

Recent findings suggest that george and I pushed off before daylight and began motoring with the current down the main ditch, No. 62, which flowed south. By dawn we’d gone about half the eight miles we intended to go. Long before we reached our goal we had seen enough flushing mallards to be reasonably sure of plenty of action. Finally we left the main ditch, No. 62, shut down the little outboard engine, and prepared to paddle west through the woods. The ducks continued to work overhead, seemingly intent on reaching the area we had chosen.

We found an ideal situation, where thick bunch brush, covered by a dense network of vines, overlooked half an acre of open water. We pushed the boat under that natural blind and broke out ports in the tangle so that we could fire from the boat. I threw six decoys into the shallow water, and the setup appeared to be ideal. The only problem was my apprehension that our limits would come too easily and quickly for the keenest sport.

Sources indicate that the ducks flew high overhead in a constant stream but paid no attention to the invitations sounded on my Turpin call. I did my utmost to make every quack, chatter or chuckle perfect, but all the birds were homing in on one small area. Obviously, some other hunters had a better setup than we did.

“George, those fellows are the lousiest callers I’ve ever heard,” I said. “But they’re getting the ducks. Those fellows doing that tooting are champs for luck!”.

Related: Historic Drought Looms Over Arkansas Duck Opener. What Few Ducks Show Up Face Heavy Pressure.

George blinked, then noted, “J.D., I hadn’t thought about it, but we can hear those jokers calling, and they’re no good.”.

“Yeah! And getting all the ducks!” I said, thoroughly disgusted. “Watch that bunch. They set their wings and are gliding straight in without circling.”.

According to recent reports, I was envious, as well as curious. In all my years of duck hunting I had never encountered a similar situation.

Industry observers note that “Those guys sound like hogs feeding and hounds running,” George stated. “And geese honking, and cows lowing!” I added.

It has been revealed that suddenly I realized why the masses of ducks were heedless. “George,” I noted. “Those are ducks doing the calling! We have been sitting here like fools, criticizing the techniques of real ducks! What a dummy I am!”.

“How do you know they’re real ducks?” George asked.

In a recent development, “How many shots have you heard?” I said. “If there were hunters over there, we would have heard them shooting.”.

Say, you’re right!” George mentioned.

“You stay here.” I suggested. “I’ll wade over and put that raft of ducks up. We can’t do any good as long as we have to compete with real ducks on the water.”.

“Wait a minute, J.D.,” George said. “Mind if I go with you? I never saw a massive bunch of ducks on the water.”.

Before George was out of sight, the ducks came back in throngs. At first I merely gave the short call and the feed call, and the birds fell through the trees and onto the water in dozens, then in hundreds.

Sources indicate that three hundred yards of wading brought us to the mallard equivalent of the famous Antoine’s restaurant in New Orleans. Under the clear three to six-inch-deep water was a golden bed of acorns. There was scant time to absorb the charm of the place because about five acres of the area before us erupted into flight. The roar of at least 20,000 beating wings is best described by George’s reaction. Plucking at my sleeve he shouted, “Let’s get out of here. That’s a tornado!”.

Sources indicate that “You can’t fool me,” he insisted. “I’m from Texas, remember? I know what tornados sound like!”.

“That’s the roar of duck wings you hear!” I stated. “Ducks are making THAT much of a roar?” he shouted. We were forced to yell in order to be heard over the noise of the wings.

In a recent development, as the ducks lifted out, the volume of sound diminished. “Where is your tornado now?” I asked.

Industry observers note that “That was unbelievable!” he said. “Simply incredible! Nobody could have made me understand that ducks could make that much noise, even if millions got up!”.

“George, this is the spot for our setup,” I mentioned. “If we had the boat and decoys here we could have a blue-ribbon shoot.”.

“Show me the direction of the boat and I’II go get it,” George said.

“OK,” I said, pointing his course. “Just keep that straight line and you can’t miss it.” He hitched his boots up in an instinctive gesture and ambled away. That decision to let George go after the boat was one of the most stupid of my mistakes. And it came nearest to being fatal.

Recent findings suggest that before George was out of sight, the ducks came back in throngs. At first I merely gave the short call and the feed call, and the birds fell through the trees and onto the water in dozens, then in hundreds. The ancient snag I leaned against provided ample cover because I remained motionless.

According to recent reports, soon the greedy mallards were feeding as though they could not gobble the acorns rapidly enough. When my foot became cramped, I shifted slowly and slightly but the wary mallards were up and away.

When some birds came back over and started circling I called them in and killed a pair. My motives were to give George a bearing. He had been away far longer than necessary and I began to be concerned.

According to recent reports, the ducks were eager to get down to the feed, so killing the limit was absurdly easy. I decided that to work the crow call would give George my location. I blew the Turpin crow call as loudly as one has ever been sounded, confident that George would hear it and know who was calling. George was not a crow shooter, but he knew, or I thought he knew, there were none in the Floodway at that time of year.

Soon I became concerned about George, blaming myself for letting him fetch the boat. He was certainly no woodsman and even less a swamp rat. Just as I was trying to decide on a course of action, I heard the slosh, slosh of his deliberate wading. That was fine, except that he was approaching from the opposite direction than I had expected. I could see him quite plainly, in my imagination, as he splashed along towing the boat. When he actually appeared without the boat, I could hardly credit my senses.

“Where did you leave the boat?” I asked.

“I never did find it,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that I felt as though I had been dealt a heavy blow between the eyes. I was dazed and disoriented. I was so thoroughly confused that I had to wade around three tall snags to find the 15 slain mallards I had tossed at the base of the big stump where I was standing. I had no idea where the boat was. The sky looked like the underside of a dark gray tent, precluding any possibility of gaining the least help from the sun. There were no traffic noises. No sound of whistles, bells or machinery was nearer than eight miles from us.

We found thousands upon thousands of wild mallards, but no trace of our six wooden decoys or any other clue to our boat’s location. As far as we were concerned, the boat had disappeared forever.

We were as hopelessly lost as though stranded in the Sahara or in forests of the Belgian Congo.

Sources indicate that I had my compass, but it was next to useless because no matter which direction we chose to follow, we could go only a short distance before we reached a deep ditch, canal or sink. All were filled with water, and we could swim across none. The only value of knowing the precise direction was to help us follow the only pathway that might wind around to provide the one route to the confluence of Ditch No. 62 and a string of borrow pits. It was there thal we just might luck onto someone in a boat, although the chance of any duck hunter being there so late in such weather was virtually nonexistent. I was scared — badly scared.

Industry observers note that without a boat we were doomed to remain in the flooded timber and die. We would become to weak to sit on a fallen tree trunk or to stand in the water, trying to balance ourselves on the muddy, uneven ground under the muddy, frigid water. Then we would freeze or drown.

Our only hope was to find our boat. We found thousands upon thousands of wild mallards, but no trace of our six wooden decoys or any other clue to our boat’s location. As far as we were concerned, the boat had disappeared forever.

This will give an indication of the futility of our search: After the ordeal I offered a trapper $10 to find the hidden boat. I explained as nearly as possible where the boat was, and he accepted the challenge. It was only after three days of careful, expert searching that he found it. He told us he’d passed within 10 yards of the craft three times — carefully following my directions — before he finally pushed the brush blind aside and found the boat.

“I never would have believed anybody could hide something as big as a boat, especially with wooden decoys floating on the water close to it, then tell me exactly where it was and I would have to look for it three days to find it,” he said.

After abandoning our search for the boat, and our last hope of escaping from the flooded woods, I told George we would have to wade to where No. 62 ditch flowed past the borrow pits.

Should we by chance reach that point, we had a very slight chance to get a ride with some duck hunters who were headed for their cars.

We knew that if we reached the confluence of the No. 62 ditch and the borrow pits we’d need a boat to cross a borrow pit at least 15 feet deep.

To try to swim to safety was out of the question, and if we made the first swim we would still be eight miles from the clubhouse with more than a dozen breaks in the levee, each a deep, swiftly flowing, icy flood. I explained all this to George.

It has been revealed that as we waded. George decided that my compass was out of kilter and that we were going in the wrong direction. Finally, after having shown him the compass half a dozen times. I asked whether he still believed the instrument to be in error, and he did.

Recent findings suggest that “All right,” I told him. “You go the right way and I will follow the compass on our present course.”.

He chose for us to stay together and, without debate, followed the compass readings from then on. George was not accustomed to conditions such as we had encountered and began to weaken. As he did, he tripped and fell. I jerked him back to his feet but he was soaked. After several falls, I became concerned about his ability to wade farther. It was then, just before dark, that George stepped into a deep stump hole and went entirely under. There was nothing to be done except to step down into the water and drag him out. By that time. I, too, was saturated and chilled to the bone, dead tired, hungry and scared witless.

The thought of being trapped in the cold with no place to rest and nothing to eat or drink. was terrifying, especially because nobody even knew just where we were. The frigid wind sought out each opening in our winter gear, probably seeping in through buttonholes. The cold water was a danger on all sides of us — and we were helpless. I could tell George was hopeless — a bad attitude for one who would survive.

Sources indicate that cold became an obsession. I was in a delirium of cold. I could think of nothing but cold and could feel nothing but cold. As night fell, the thought of us alone, helpless, in the water, in the cold, almost overcame me. I knew the feeling of coming face-to-face with death in its grimmest, most terrifying aspect.

Industry observers note that sudden death by such violence as an explosion, even death by tire, painful as it would be. seemed lesser punishment than this protracted end after countless hours of excruciating agony.

According to recent reports, terror overcame me time after time. But to give way to fear or to cold would be to die. and I could not afford to die.

During my many misadventures in the outdoors, I have been petrified with fright and agonized by injuries. One time I spent a night under an ice cake in the middle of the Mississippi River. I thought that experience was the worst mixture of pain and panic I had ever endured, or could ever survive. But now I knew how mistaken such an assessment could be before one has been ground by the mills of chance into finer fiber.

Industry observers note that it was fortunate for us that a large tree had been felled and the butt had not fallen from the stump. I helped George up on to the horizontal tree trunk and, with my knife, gouged a small depression in the dead wood. Into this saucer I placed some duck down and small wood chips.

I could feel nothing but pain with my badly frozen hands. I opened some shells and poured the powder over the makeshift kindling. Then, by wading from tree to tree and breaking off dead branches hanging above the water, I finally got enough fuel for a tiny fire. With freezing hands I fumbled my waterproof matchbox from a frozen pocket. The contraption contained 25 dry kitchen matches. The first 17 were extinguished instantly by the wind, despite my best efforts to prevent it. The 18th match kindled the flame. The only way I could hold a wooden match was by clasping it with the tongue in my duck call, a poor tool for that, but far better then my numb hands.

“George, I am going to continue to bring dry sticks,” I explained. “But do not build a massive blaze. The small fire will enable us to get close, almost over it, and absorb some warmth. A big fire will only drive us back and most of the heat will go to waste over our heads.”.

“All right, J. D.,” he chattered, placing every piece of wood on the leaping flames as soon as he could get his eager hands on it. And so it went; I brought a pile of sticks during the next few hours and George burned all of them, to the smallest twig, as soon as he could reach them.

George had a death grip on his good grade, double-barrel gun, but I was concerned that it might fall from his grasp. l cut a stout little twig about four inches out from a tree trunk and hung my gun, also a double, by the trigger guard, using the projecting bit of the lopped-off branch. I suggested that George let me do the same for his gun, before he dropped it.

“It doesn’t matter,” he said, “I’II never live to use it again anyway.”.

I persuaded him that his heirs might be able to sell such a handsome weapon, proceeded to cut a small rack for his gun, took it from his nerveless fingers, and hung it from the tree.

It has been revealed that ducks were in the water on all sides of us, and they were noisy. Each time a susie quacked or a drake wheezed, George would mutter and mumble. Finally he burst out: “Damn the ducks! Damn all ducks!”.

“Why, George, J thought that you liked ducks and duck talk,” I teased. That night was the only time I ever heard him say an oath. “I hate the things!” he mentioned. “If l ever get out of here, alive, I will never hunt ducks again!”.

I’d never heard him say anything with more vehemence.

“J.D. !” George stated. “We will have pneumonia as a result of this exposure. We’ll be sick as the devil, too. The crisis will occur on the fifth day, (that was long before penicillin and antibiotics), then after another forty-eight hours we will be dead.” His tone was so lugubrious that I laughed.

“You may be getting pneumonia, but I am not,” I assured him.

“As a physician, I have seen it happen too often,” he said, not to be dissuaded.

“Nuts to pneumonia!” I said. “I’m not interested in anything except to get off this log.”.

In a recent development, “We will probably survive tonight and perhaps tomorrow,” George said. “Perhaps by tomorrow night we will become so weak that we will fall in the water and die of hypothermia, called exposure.” A bright prospect, I thought, as George continued, “Well, I am ready to go at any time. My life insurance is adequate and is paid up. I have nobody but my wife and she will be well provided for … He had it all worked out, and was speaking sincerely when he said he was resigned to perish.

“Well, my wife and two tiny tots will still need some care,” I responded, “and I, my boy, intend to stick around a while to provide it!” I had never spoken more earnestly.

I thought that George had dozed as he slumped on the log, since he had not put a stick on the fire for almost a full minute, but an unusually raucous outburst of quacks from a startled mallard hen caused him to shout, “Damn those ducks! To hell with all ducks! If I ever get out of here alive I will never hunt ducks again!”.

Right then I heard something in the distance.

Industry observers note that “George! Do you hear what I do?” I demanded.

“Sounds like someone running an outboard engine,” he stammered between chattering teeth.

“Exactly.” I was excited as I loaded his gun and handed it to him. “He is coming down sixty-two ditch. When he gets to the end of the ditch, he’ II shut his engine down. Let’s wait about thirty seconds after it stops, to let him get the ringing out of his ears. Then let’s shoot our guns and yell like hell!”.

Sources indicate that the engine sputtered and was silent. The waiting seemed eternal as I counted 30 seconds off. It was then 9 o’clock, our rescuer told me later. Then we shot our guns and yelled like demons! Ducks spattered off the water from quite near.

A voice hailed. We replied. I shouted that we were stranded. After a long interval we could hear a push pule thumping and scraping, then a headlamp came into view, moving slowly along the deep water. The light stopped quite a long way from us.

“Air you’uns them fellers fum Me’phis what we’uns is come after?” came the question.

“Well, push yore boat outen th’woods so’s we’uns kin holp you’uns outen th’ cold.”.

It has been revealed that “Whut happent? Run hit onter uh cypus knee?” our would-be rescuer queried.

“No,” I yelped. “We just lost our boat!”.

The light moved back another dozen yards.

“Lost hit? How cud no boat git lost?” he demanded suspiciously. “Hain ‘t hardly no way tuh jes lose uh boat!”.

“Look, we lost the boat and are freezing. Come and get us, please!”  My voice echoed my desperation and the boatman decided that we were harmless, after all.

He pushed his boat up to our log and I helped George aboard. The eight-mile run into the teeth of the wind was the worst three-hour ordeal I have ever suffered. Our wet clothing was frozen solid before we had gone halfway. When we docked at the clubhouse our frozen clothing was rigid and we were immobilized, encased in ice. Two men were required to lift each of us to the dock.

Read Next: Where Are All the Ducks?

Sources indicate that mr. Ambrose, who had sent our rescuer, was ready with his brandy bottle. We followed the brandy with cup after cup of scalding coffee. As we sat huddled over a substantial meal, our first of the day, we were so near the big stove that steam from our drying clothing obscured our vision. George fanned the cloud of steam from in front of his face, and, peering anxiously, asked, “J.D. can you make it over here again Wednesday?”.

It was then one o’clock Monday morning. He would never hunt ducks again — until Wednesday morning, that is.

Industry News: Expert Tips for Patterning and Hunting a Late-Season Buck

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1210 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that beaten, bruised, and a bit smarter than it was on opening day, the old buck slowly moves from his bed.
  • Keeping it in low gear, the deer alternates between taking a couple steps and scanning its surroundings.
  • Sitting high in a tall cedar tree, you wait for any sign of the significant 10-pointer you’ve been after all season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that beaten, bruised, and a bit smarter than it was on opening day, the old buck slowly moves from his bed. The sun just set, but he’s not anywhere close to a significant field yet.

Keeping it in low gear, the deer alternates between taking a couple steps and scanning its surroundings. On pins and pine needles, the buck nears the edge of the bedding area, hits a smaller trail other deer rarely use, and sets course for the distant standing soybean field.

Sitting high in a tall cedar tree, you wait for any sign of the significant 10-pointer you’ve been after all season. Any moment now….

In a recent development, suddenly, you see the front legs of a deer standing in the timber on the hill above. Seconds turn into minutes, and the deer doesn’t move. Finally, it covers a few more yards, and that big 10-point rack comes into view. Only 50 yards separate the late-season hunter and the buck — all because he focused on patterning a late-season buck. Here’s how to do it.

Recent findings suggest that some elements of patterning a late-season deer take place before the hunt. It’s a good time to reassess the situation, reflect on the past, and take a new approach.

Recent findings suggest that hunt fresh spots. Late-season deer are especially wary. At this point in the season, some deer have been shot and shot at. Virtually all deer have felt pressure, so it’s crucial to spend some time scouting areas that weren’t hunted previously. Oftentimes, it’s these places deer slink into during the late season. Even if these spots seem less than perfect, it’s worth scouting them.

Reflect on the Past: Consider past seasons and how deer behaved then. Refer to trail camera intel and sightings of deer in the field. Digging into the details of past seasons will help you understand current and future deer movement. If conditions and habitat factors and food sources line up similarly to how they have in the past, deer should exhibit similar patterns. This takes a lot of the guesswork out of game planning.

Recent findings suggest that effective deer hunting is all about knowing whitetail lines of movement. Studying the lines that take whitetails from point A to point B is crucial for selecting a high-odds stand or blind location.

Industry observers note that locate the food. Food drives late-season deer behavior. Locate the food, and you find the deer. That said, deer place emphasis on the limiting resource factor. If safe bedding cover is scarce, they’ll find what’s available and travel farther to reach food. If safe bedding cover is abundant, they’ll bed closer to the available food.

According to recent reports, hunt a late-season kill plot. It’s too late to plant now, but if you planted a late-season food plot, it’s time to cash in. Standing corn, standing soybeans, winter wheat, turnips, and much more, make excellent late-season food sources for whitetails. Placing a winter food plot in a strategic location, such as near solar or thermal bedding cover, is a solid play. It can make the patterning process much easier.

Save a food plot. As fall gives way to winter, and food sources wane, deer hammer what’s left. The only way to keep a food plot viable into the late season is to prevent deer and other critters from consuming it earlier. That requires planting the right plant species (like brassicas), keeping deer out (with an electric exclusion fence), and opening it up at just the right time. Thus, you’re saving a food plot for the final days of the season.

In a recent development, find the thermal bedding. Deer use certain types of bedding cover to combat the winter cold. The most common is thermal bedding (especially in flatter areas without much topography). This comes in the form of cedars, spruce, and pine trees. These evergreens shield deer from the rain, sleet, and snow. Furthermore, these thick plants block bitter-cold winds. Equally impressive is that the air temperature is several degrees warmer amidst the conifers.

Recent findings suggest that identify south-facing slopes. Deer also benefit significantly from the sun. Because the winter sun rises in the southeast, and sets in the southwest, the southerly face of the slope will be warmer on sunny days. So long as deer aren’t pressured there, it should be the primary deer bedding spot for the general area.

Glass from afar. Even in today’s world of cellular trail cameras, the age-old tactic of sitting down and raising the glasses is still a good one. You’ll need open country like fields that serve as primary food sources.

Recent findings suggest that watch a buck’s route. To pattern a deer is to know its general whereabouts and habits. These include bedding areas, food sources, water sources, staging areas, and the travel routes in between. By watching a buck’s route in person, scouting for tracks, or monitoring via trail cameras, hunters can watch a buck’s route and make firm aims after identifying the target.

In a recent development, reposition trail cameras. While in the field scouting for deer sign, positioning stands, filling feeders, and completing other tasks, go ahead and set up some new trail camera locations. Where legal, focus on the cellular variety. If cameras that were productive early season have gone dead now, don’t be afraid to move them to more promising spots.

After determining your target buck’s lines of movement, it’s time to make a move. Put the strategy in motion, or call an audible as needed.

Recent findings suggest that still hunt the edges. While still hunting works best during the rut when deer are more distracted, it can be effective during the late season, too. If you’ve had trouble patterning a late-season buck, consider still hunting. Moving slowly, yet covering ground, might help piece together remaining clues to hunt a deer you know about, or help find a latest one altogether. Still hunting is especially effective for morning hunts, when it’s often difficult to hike straight into a stand location without spooking deer.

Read Next: The Case for Ditching Your Treestand and Hunting from the Ground.

In a recent development, track down your buck. A fresh blanket of snow makes for prime tracking conditions, and if you have an idea about a buck’s travel lines, tracking becomes a lot easier. Go slow, and keep your eyes peeled. Chances are good he’ll see you first, but move slowly enough, and you’ll have a chance at a shot.

Be mobile and flexible. Whether you are hunting from a treestand, hunting blind, or still hunting through cover, remember to be flexible. Be patient and execute your proposal, but don’t be so attached that it stays in motion even after it becomes clear another tactic is better. Remember that each deer hunt is its own unique experience. Thus, hunters should always implement tactics based on the situation.

Industry observers note that late-season deer hunting is no cakewalk. Deer are skittish and the bitter cold can be tough to endure. Nonetheless, hunt hard, and you just might bag a buck. Focus on new, unpressured spots, protected bedding areas, and primary food sources to finally punch that buck tag.

Savvy shoppers know Black Friday is the Super Bowl of savings. These days, it’s more like Black Friday Week, which gives us even more time to browse the best deals.

For skiers, there’s no better time to refresh your gear closet than November, when you start taking stock of what you own and what you need for the season. The good news is that Evo is a one-stop shop for everything from hard goods to travel bags, and the deals are plentiful. Keep reading to see what the SKI team is recommending from Evo’s significant Black Friday sale.

We’ll admit it’s not the sexiest gift on anyone’s list, but Evo’s Roller Ski Bag is on sale, and it’s a no-brainer for ski travelers who want to bring their own skis and ensure they arrive safely at their destination. The bag has wheels, which is essential for hauling skis through airports and parking lots. It also holds up to two pairs of skis, poles, boots, outerwear, and accessories, all in padded, durable compartments. Internal straps keep everything in place, and the bag folds up for compact storage between trips. —Samantha Berman.

I’ve long appreciated the Arc’teryx Sentinel for its clean, understated design and thoughtful features. It’s a serious technical shell without a lot of unnecessary bells and whistles, and the weather protection is hard to beat.

Industry observers note that what I especially like is the longer, freeride-inspired silhouette, which provides plenty of coverage over my hips and works well with bibs. The fit feels streamlined without being restrictive, and I can comfortably wear a lightweight puffy underneath on colder days. When the weather turns, the three-layer GORE-TEX construction and helmet-compatible StormHood help seal out wind and snow.

In a recent development, the latest Sentinel has been updated with a tougher 100-denier face fabric, a refined fit, larger hand pockets, and a newly introduced chest pocket. It’s also designed for moving between the resort and backcountry, which is exactly the kind of versatility I look for in a shell.

According to recent reports, the fabric is on the stiffer side, especially when new, and takes a little time to break in. But it isn’t excessively loud or crunchy, and I appreciate that rugged feel in a jacket designed for years of hard use. The Sentinel is a significant investment, so finding one on sale makes it a lot more appealing. —Sierra Shafer.

I’m a massive fan of getting dressed for skiing in the lodge instead of the parking lot, so I’m usually hauling my skis, boots, and assorted gear from the car. The Yardsale Day Bag makes that whole process a lot easier.

Sources indicate that at 30 liters, it’s roomy enough to fit everything I need without becoming a bottomless black hole. The magnetic closures, internal divider, dedicated pockets, and key ring help keep smaller items organized, while the cinch closure makes it easy to throw in bulkier gear without worrying about things falling out. There’s even a padded laptop sleeve for days when I’m working from the mountain and hoping to sneak in a few lunch laps.

According to recent reports, one of my favorite details is the suitcase sleeve, which lets me slide the bag securely over my rolling carry-on when I travel. No more tote bag constantly slipping off my shoulder or luggage at the airport.

Sources indicate that it’s also plenty durable. I’ve shoved it under countless lodge tables, dragged it around on trips, and even spilled what appears to have been an entire glass of red wine inside it. Most of the evidence came out in the wash, and I still reach for this bag constantly. —SS.

It has been revealed that I’m firmly in the mittens-over-gloves camp. They’re warmer, more comfortable, and I’ve been skiing in Oyuki mittens for years. I’ve worn every pair I’ve owned until the insulation eventually packed out, usually after four or five seasons of heavy use. That kind of longevity has made me a loyal fan.

The Sencho GORE-TEX mittens combine waterproof protection with warm PrimaLoft insulation and a soft wool lining. What I especially like about OYUKI mittens is how supple and comfortable they feel, without the excessive bulk that can make some mittens frustrating to wear. I can still manage poles, zippers, and most of the little tasks that come up throughout a ski day without constantly taking them off.

The wrist coverage helps eliminate that annoying gap between your mittens and jacket sleeves, while the leashes mean I can pull them off on the chairlift without worrying about losing one.

I also love the brand’s Japanese roots. Oyuki means “big snow,” and the kanji in its logo translates to “smash pow.” How can you not love that? —SS.

When I reach for an insulated jacket on a resort ski day, odds are high it’s the Halfdays Georgie puffer. It’s one of the brand’s original styles, and it’s a classic for a reason. The 550-fill body is warm without being bulky, and the 15,000mm waterproof rating keeps you dry all day on a powder day. My favorite features are the pockets, which were clearly designed by people who ski: they’re intuitively placed and even come with a goggle wipe and a phone leash. The snap-removable hood fits over practically every helmet, too. The dark green colorway is right now on sale, and it just so happens to be on my wishlist.

Evo is also offering a bundle deal for the Georgie Puffer and Alessandra Pants for $644 (down from $920) —Jamie Aranoff.

Industry observers note that the Hydra Thermagraph delivers impressive performance and style for the price, making it one of the better values in women’s ski outerwear—especially at its Black Friday discount. It pairs a waterproof, breathable 20K infiDRY shell with Thermagraph body-mapped insulation that puts warmth where you need it rather than throughout. Add in features including underarm vents, a helmet-compatible hood, a powder skirt, and generous pockets—including a dedicated phone heater pocket—and you’ve got a jacket that can handle everything from frigid chairlift rides to deep powder days. —SB.

The Stio Pinion Down Hooded Jacket is one of those versatile layers that earns its keep well beyond ski season. Its lightweight, packable design and water-resistant 800-fill HyperDRY down make it an excellent layer under a shell, adding warmth without unnecessary bulk. The clean, casual styling also makes it a solid everyday grab for walking the dog, running errands, or grabbing après beers. It’s a worthwhile Black Friday upgrade for the minimalist on your list who doesn’t like to waste closet space. —SB.

In a recent development, I first fell for the Head Kore 94 at SKI Test, and it has promptly become one of my favorites. It carried me through Utah’s unusually warm winter, when I needed a ski that wasn’t afraid of a little ice. On the few powder days we did get, it stayed afloat better than expected, and never felt like it was sinking. It’s a jack of all trades, which is exactly what I want in a daily driver. The 2027 model is out now, but there’s not a huge change from 2026, so snagging these for under $400 is a win. —JA.

You can read the full review here.

Industry observers note that the Cotopaxi Tasra 16L Backpack hits the sweet spot as a ski-day pack: compact enough to stay out of your way on the lift, but roomy enough to carry the essentials, from an extra layer and snacks to water, sunscreen, and other necessities. Its 16-liter capacity keeps you from overstuffing it, while multiple pockets, dual water-bottle sleeves, and a durable recycled-polyester construction make it a practical choice. —SB.

It has been revealed that kari Traa makes base layers for the girls who shred. I absolutely love my sets from this brand, founded by an Olympian, and I find that the capri pants never slip down, which is seriously important when it comes to successful layering. These 100-percent merino wool pieces will keep you warm all day, and when you start to sweat, they’ll keep you dry, too. Mix and match patterns for a fun base layer that’ll last for many seasons to come. —JA.

According to recent reports, I’ve skied almost exclusively in Le Bent socks for years, and the Compression Zero Cushion is a favorite. It took me a while to come around to compression socks, but now I appreciate the supportive fit, especially on long days in ski boots.

Sources indicate that I prefer a really thin ski sock because I like being able to feel my boot, and Le Bent’s blend of merino wool and bamboo-derived rayon does an excellent job managing moisture. There’s a misconception that thicker socks are always warmer, but a thin, moisture-wicking sock helps keep your feet dry, which goes a long way toward keeping them warm. And in a snug ski boot, extra bulk can compromise fit and circulation.

The compression is noticeable without feeling restrictive, and the socks stay put all day. No sliding, no bunching, no annoying wrinkles inside my boots, even when I’m touring and moving around a lot more than I would on a resort day.

I also appreciate the height. I have long legs, and these come up high enough to meet my three-quarter-length base layers without leaving an uncomfortable gap of bare skin. They may not technically be on sale at evo this Black Friday, but I’m still taking the reminder to repurchase before ski season starts in earnest.—SS.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1328 w)

Latest Update: The 7 Most Desperate Things I’ve Done in My Search for Ski Boots That Fit

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1328 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Seven states, two countries, three acupuncturists, and one orthopedist later, a skier with hard-to-fit feet found the bootfitter she needed.
  • Overview: This first-person essay follows one skier’s years-long search for ski boots that fit, with bootfitters in seven states and two countries, a visit to an orthopedist, three acupuncturists, and a stranger’s garage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Seven states, two countries, three acupuncturists, and one orthopedist later, a skier with hard-to-fit feet found the bootfitter she needed. (Photo: Courtesy Abigail Barronian).

Overview: This first-person essay follows one skier’s years-long search for ski boots that fit, with bootfitters in seven states and two countries, a visit to an orthopedist, three acupuncturists, and a stranger’s garage. It’s a funny account of what hard-to-fit feet can drive a person to do, and a reminder that the right bootfitter can change everything.

In my quest for ski boots that fit, I’ve seen bootfitters in at least seven states and two countries. I’ve visited Evo and REI, small independent shops, local chains, and garages-turned-ski shops. I’ve consulted boot designers, brand reps, professional athletes, and gear reviewers; tried Intuitions, ZipFits, and custom footbeds. I’ve seen one orthopedic doctor, three acupuncturists, and two physical therapists. I’ve stayed up at night thinking about boots, and developed recurring stress dreams about them.

According to recent reports, last season, I was beginning to consider looping in a tarot reader or astrologer. Maybe I needed a psychotherapist, or a priest. Maybe I’d have to just quit skiing. And then, finally, I found my bootfitter. But not before resorting to some questionable behavior along the way. Here are seven desperate things I did in my search for a bootfitter who could solve my ski boot issues.

According to recent reports, every pair of ski boots I wore from ages two through 22 were hand-me-downs from my older brothers. Then I started working in the ski industry. While skiing around Significant Sky during a media event, a kind man working for Nordica looked at my feet with a frown.

“What are those?” he asked. I was sliding around in some decade-old size 26.5 monstrosities. He shook his head and invited me to swing by the Nordica headquarters in New Hampshire. There, he measured my feet and sent me off with a pair of 25.5 Nordica Promachines.

In a recent development, everything changed. Suddenly I was in an aggressive stance, my shins met real resistance, my power transfer improved dramatically. I got a taste of what a good boot can do, shortly before developing a wicked case of tendonitis in my ankles and shins.

According to recent reports, after two seasons of excruciating, day-ending pain, I booked an appointment with an orthopedic foot and ankle specialist. I knew my boots were the culprit, and couldn’t be sure a doctor would understand the whole foot-encased-in-rigid-plastic thing. I lugged a giant bag with both my alpine and touring boots into the orthopedic practice and pulled them out for show-and-tell.

Sources indicate that the physician kindly assured me he knew what ski boots were, and that I wasn’t dealing with any serious medical complications. I’d have to take my boots back where they belonged.

The owner of Santa Fe’s one dedicated ski shop sized me down yet again, into the stiffest 24.5 he had on hand—a 110 from Fischer. I felt like I was skiing in socks and a vise-grip at the same time, and I lost feeling in my feet on the first lap. Mercifully, he let me return them.

In a recent development, I’d hit the central problem: boots massive enough to be comfortable gave me tendonitis, and boots small enough to prevent it gave me bunions and nerve pain. So I took my boots to Taos Bootdoctors, where a whole team of bootfitters worked patiently to expand the forefoot. I’d ski for a day or two and come back, over and over, looking for just a few more millimeters. I brought six-packs and did my best to be charming, and the lovely staff never made me feel less important than the tourists dropping thousands of dollars on gear. Still, I couldn’t finish a day without pain.

Recent findings suggest that I soldiered through the season, eyeing an upcoming hut trip with dread. I could manage shorter tours, but a week of daylong missions posed some real problems. Once we were in the mountains, I knew no amount of bunion donuts and anti-inflammatories would save me. I had to instate boots-off breaks in the middle of eight-hour ski days, carefully pulling my socked feet out of jail and propping them up on a backpack in the snow while my friends took an extra lap. Sweet, stupid relief.

Sources indicate that finally, I heard a rumor about a man in Seattle working out of his garage who was willing to do unorthodox things to ski boots. He had a history of custom-fitting plug boots for ski racers, which seemed like a good sign. While visiting family in Washington, I brought him both pairs of boots.

Sources indicate that he looked at my feet, listened patiently, and rattled off a comprehensive strategy that involved several devices I’d never seen before. Overnight, he molded both pairs into a completely newly introduced shape. I never had to touch either boot again, and proceeded with great pleasure to ski 12-hour days in the backcountry and endless resort laps with happy feet. I had found him—the bootfitter I was looking for. Then, he retired.

According to recent reports, when my touring boots started to go, I bought a replacement pair and nobody could make them fit. The experience began to take on mythic proportions. I felt like the princess with a pea beneath her many mattresses, or an ugly stepsister trying to cram her foot into a crystal slipper: all discomfort and wrong fit.

It seemed my trusty Tecnicas were the problem. I tried on every touring boot at ski shops in three states. I ordered over a dozen pairs online, obsessively double-checking return policies and momentarily racking up a very scary credit card bill. Eventually, I came crawling back to my old Tecnicas with no plan, two full seasons into the search.

In a recent development, I hesitated to say yes to ski trips, afraid I’d have to sit out ski days because of pain or busted gear. Eventually, it happened: I took my tired old touring boots to Rogers Pass in B.C. and, on day three, broke the upper cuff clean off the bottom section of the boot. Thankfully we were just a few hundred yards from the truck. I spent the entire day sitting at the trailhead.

Industry observers note that in the meantime, my alpine boots had begun to warp. I found a replacement pair and was back at square one: home in Upcoming Mexico, with two pairs of ski boots that didn’t fit, rapidly dwindling patience, and no bootfitter.

Sources indicate that I considered that this might be the end of the road for me as a skier. Then, I learned that one of the best skiers I know had been contemplating quitting the sport because of foot pain. He’d even gone so far as to teach himself to snowboard. But then he found exactly what I’d been looking for: yet another fit-obsessed industry veteran working out of his garage.

I visited another home workshop in western Washington and the bootfitter listened carefully as I explained the glitch. Then, he overhauled both pairs of boots, tirelessly stretching the forefoots to give my feet room to breathe. They took on a completely newly introduced shape: generous and wide. I took both pairs out for a spin and sighed in relief.

Industry observers note that there are a lot of great bootfitters out there. But for a freak like me, I’ve learned I need something of a mad scientist. If you’re plagued with bone spurs, high insteps, wide feet—there’s hope, I promise. With a little faith, a lot of persistence, and maybe something like divine intervention, I trust you’ll find the bootfitter you need. Let’s just hope they don’t retire.

#205262. Controversial Senate Bill Would Speed Up Development on Public Lands

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1761 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fieldandstream ↗ Open Full Page

Controversial Senate Bill Would Speed Up Development on Public Lands

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1761 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On November 19, the United State Senate passed a sweeping 400-page bill with big implications for America’s federally managed public lands.
  • Industry observers note that co-sponsored by Sen.
  • Recent findings suggest that A large portion of the bill aims to reform or streamline the permitting process that developers must adhere to when applying for projects on federal public lands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On November 19, the United State Senate passed a sweeping 400-page bill with big implications for America’s federally managed public lands. Called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act—or BAAJA for short—the bill would ease permitting restrictions for all sorts of public-land development projects, from mining and drilling to large-scale solar farms and geothermal power projects. Supporters say it would open the door for more clean-energy projects on public lands while reducing utility costs for American consumers.

Industry observers note that co-sponsored by Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-NM) and Sen. Mike Lee (R-UT), BAAJA has drawn widespread criticism from conservationists, environmentalists, and public land advocates, with groups from the Wilderness Society to the National Wildlife Federation speaking out in opposition. According to the National Council of American Indians, it has also caused serious concerns in tribal nations across the country.

Recent findings suggest that A large portion of the bill aims to reform or streamline the permitting process that developers must adhere to when applying for projects on federal public lands. It would do so by shrinking the scope, timelines, and legal challenges currently available under both the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the Clean Water Act (CWA).

In an October blog post, the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership (TRCP) said “permitting reform rules decide how a pipeline, transmission line, mine or dam gets approved, whether hunters and anglers have any say in where it goes—and what happens to elk winter range, trout streams or migration corridors in their path.”.

While TRCP has stopped short of publicly opposing the bill, they did highlight several concerns in the post. For starters, they flagged a provision in the bill—Section 1401—that “would make it much more challenging to fix problems once a project is permitted.”.

Titled “Project Certainty,” this section of the BAAJA bill would restrict federal agencies—like the Bureau of Land Management or the US Forest Service—from revoking previously issued permits during future presidential administrations. Critics say this section of the bill could lock in controversial projects—like a proposed copper-sulfide mine on the edge of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness or the 211-mile Ambler mining road that the Department of the Interior (DOI) is pushing for Alaska’s Brooks Range.

It has been revealed that in a separate blog post, Backcountry Hunters & Anglers (BHA) highlighted similar concerns with the “Project Certainty” provision in the BAAJA bill. “For BHA, this raises questions about whether federal land managers would retain sufficient flexibility to respond to changing conditions and protect public resources over the long term,” the BHA post states. “For example, if a mining project near Minnesota’s Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness received federal approval, these provisions could limit a future administration’s ability to revisit that approval in response to newly identified impacts on water quality or fisheries, depending on the circumstances and applicable legal exceptions.”.

It has been revealed that aaron Kindle is the Director of Sporting Advocacy at the National Wildlife Federation (NWF). He tells Field & Stream that NWF opposes the BAAJA bill in its current form because it raises too many questions, is moving too fast without adequate public awareness, and it undermines key public-land safeguards.

“This is a hugely consequential bill happening during a lame-duck session with very little public understanding,” Kindle notes. “[NWF] is pro-permitting reform. But when we do the analysis on this, and we talk to other conservation friends and partners, it’s just too fraught.”.

Recent findings suggest that kindle indicates NWF shares both BHA’s and TRCP’s concerns around the bill’s project certainty guarantees for developers. “It shortens review timelines, it narrows what triggers a review, and it kind of locks it in once it’s done,” he says. “We’ve always wanted to be able to do adaptive management on anything that’s done. Anytime you narrow environmental review parameters like this, or make permits too concrete, that’s concerning for a broad swath of our most cherished public lands and waters.”.

According to recent reports, kindle says NWF is also worried that the bill could expedite data center construction on public lands. Up until now, no data center has been permitted on any federal public lands, though the DOI did attempt to approve one on BLM lands in Nevada back in August, before a federal appeals court revoked the permit.

In a recent development, “What we’ve understood so far is that [BAAJA] shields [data center developers] from future regulations and makes it hard, or maybe even impossible, to revoke the permits once they’ve been awarded,” he adds. “What if we learn at some future point that these things are incredibly harmful to water, air, wildlife, the grid, who knows—and then they’re just locked in place, and there’s nothing we can do about it?”.

The Wilderness Society has been one of the most vocal opponents of the BAAJA bill since it first started making headlines in early November. Wilderness Society President, Tracy Stone-Manning, who ran the BLM during the Biden Administration, calls the bill alarming.

“Some of the places that hang in the balance are the Boundary Waters in northern Minnesota and the Brooks Range of Alaska, because of the proposed Ambler Road and Arctic Mine, the entire Alaskan Arctic really, and all of that caribou habitat,” Stone-Manning tells F&S. “You’ve also got places in the Lower 48, like the Roan Plateau in Colorado with its amazing mule deer and elk herds, which sportsmen and women fought so hard to protect, and the headwaters of Montana’s Bitterroot River, where they want to build a rare-earth mine up on Sheep Creek. Whatever the Trump Administration decides to do in these places in the next two years, that gets locked in if this bill passes. We won’t be able to undo it.”.

The Wilderness Society supports expanded permitting for renewable energy projects on public lands, which have declined steeply during the first two years of the Trump Administration. But for Stone-Manning, the risks of the BAAJA bill far outweigh the rewards.

Industry observers note that “The bottom line is, this bill takes away environmental safeguards for habitat and gives developers certainty,” she says. “Those two things coupled together spell disaster for our country’s conservation heritage and for our public-land hunting and fishing traditions.”.

Many conservationists who opposes BAAJA are confused by Sen. Martin Heinrich’s staunch support for the bill. Heinrich has been one of the Senate’s most stalwart defenders of public lands for years. He has helped secure Wilderness Area and National Monument status for thousands of acres of public lands in his home state of New Mexico, for example. More recently, he was a vocal and outspoken opponent of an attempt to sell off more than 3.4 million acres of Western public lands in the “One Big Beautiful Bill.”.

Today, he’s defending BAAJA in the halls of Congress and in the op-ed pages of major news outlets like the New York Times and the Economist. In a recent interview with Field & Stream, Heinrich cited an urgent need to slow climate change as his primary motivator for helping craft and co-sponsoring the legislation.

“This will allow us to put green energy on the grid at a scale where we might be able to mitigate the worst future outcomes of climate change,” Heinrich notes. “I’ve realized that I’m watching the world change at such a pace, that if we don’t get to work on this, I don’t know what kind of world my grandkids are going to inherit. The places that I fish in Upcoming Mexico, for example, are changing. We don’t have a lot of water. If these places go away, and we don’t have snowpack, we’re done. It’s game over.”.

Recent findings suggest that heinrich claims the bill address climate change by putting public land renewable projects—like wind, solar, and geothermal—on equal footing with oil, gas, and mining. “We want to bring renewables into the same regulatory permitting regime that the fossil fuel projects already have,” he says. “Right now, oil and gas in particular, and natural gas pipelines, have a sort of privileged position.”.

Recent findings suggest that heinrich disputes claims from his critics that the bill weakens key public-land safeguards like NEPA and the Clean Water Act. And he notes it won’t expedite or lock-in mining permits in the Boundary Waters.

In a recent development, “We don’t change or lower standards in this bill; we streamline the process,” he says. “If you’re a mine developer, you still have to get your Clean Water Act permit, and it doesn’t change the standard for that. When you look at the Boundary Waters, what I don’t see is that project being able to clear is a state Clean Water Act permit, because I just don’t think it will be possible to do mining with open-air tailings at that site—having seen it with my own eyes—without the acid generated making it into the water next door.”.

Heinrich also disagrees with BAAJA opponents who say the bill will open the door for data center development on public lands. “I don’t think that data centers belong on public lands, and I think any effort to build them on public lands is probably a legal stretch of existing authorizations and presidential authorities,” he adds. “This bill just makes data centers pay their fair freight for attaching to the grid, instead of passing that cost on to everyday consumers in the form higher electricity rates.”.

The Trump Administration’s current policy around data centers is murky at best. But recent reporting from the Washington Sun revealed that the BLM was reviewing at least 12 data center proposals spread across 17,600 acres of public land in six western states. In its recent strategic initiative, DOI, which manages close to 500 million acres of public land, listed data center development as a top priority, alongside the potential transfer or sale of federal public lands to states and local governments.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) tried to attach an amendment to the bill that would have banned the construction of data centers on public lands altogether when the Senate was debating BAAJA earlier this month. That effort ultimately failed and Wyden voted against the bill, though it still passed the full Senate on 63-33 vote.

President Trump endorsed the bill in a recent Truth Social post and said he’ll sign it if it comes across his desk, calling it a major win for energy independence and dominance. Now its awaiting a vote in the US House of Representatives. House members could vote as early as next week, when they return from Thanksgiving recess.

10 Ski Run Drop-Ins That Require Serious Nerve

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Jackson Hole).

It has been revealed that every expert skier knows this feeling: You’re standing at the top of a run, skis pointed downhill, looking over an entrance that suddenly seems a whole lot steeper than it did from the lift. Maybe there’s a cornice to negotiate, a narrow rock-lined chute to squeeze through, or a cliff that requires a leap of faith. The remainder of the run beyond the drop-in might be flat, for all you know, but getting to it is the challenge of the day.

Recent findings suggest that whatever the obstacle, some ski runs are intimidating before you even make your first turn. From legendary massive-mountain lines to tight, technical chutes, these 10 North American drop-ins are guaranteed to get your heart pumping. Consider them inspiration for the season ahead—or a reminder that sometimes it’s perfectly fine to admire the view from above.

Sources indicate that *Conditions and snow depth greatly affect how skiable the following runs are at any given time. Check trail status and heed all warnings and closures before dropping in.

In a recent development, it’s hard to make a list like this without kicking it off with Corbet’s. Perhaps the most famous—and most photographed—ski entrance in North America, this Jackson Hole icon requires skiers to negotiate a rocky cornice before dropping roughly 10 to 20 feet into a narrow, steep couloir. The landing can be soft powder or unforgiving hardpack, depending on conditions, and there’s often a crowd gathered above to watch the action. No pressure. There’s even an entire event dedicated to how stylish—or catastrophic—skiers navigate this tricky entrance.

Industry observers note that think Corbet’s is intimidating? Meet its even scarierl next-door neighbor. Located just skier’s left of Corbet’s, S&S features a mandatory cliff drop of up to 25 feet, followed by a tight landing and a narrow couloir. Skiers need to make a midair adjustment to line up the landing, leaving little room for error. This one is strictly for the seriously experienced.

According to recent reports, the name doesn’t undersell it. Big Sky’s legendary Big Couloir begins with an exposed, rocky entrance that can involve negotiating a cornice before dropping into a narrow, sustained chute. With pitches approaching 50 degrees and a 1,400-foot descent below, it’s a serious commitment from the first turn. Access is controlled by ski patrol, and skiers must check in and carry avalanche safety equipment.

Alyeska doesn’t do subtle when it comes to steep terrain, and Christmas Chute is a perfect example. The entrance funnels skiers between imposing rock walls before opening into a steep, confined chute. The line averages roughly 45 degrees and drops about 1,500 vertical feet. It’s an intimidating entrance in a spectacularly Alaskan setting, where the mountains are massive and the consequences are real.

Even the name is enough to make you think twice. The Coffin is a notorious narrow passage in Whistler’s alpine terrain, where skiers squeeze through a tight, rock-lined opening before dropping into the terrain below. Visible from the Peak Chair—but not officially on the trail map—it’s also a popular spectator attraction. The confined entrance leaves little room to get comfortable, making the moment you drop in particularly memorable.

It has been revealed that palisades Tahoe has no shortage of intimidating terrain, but McConkey’s is among its signature tests of nerve. This steep, rocky feature demands commitment from the entrance, with exposed terrain and little margin for error. The line’s reputation is part of what makes it so compelling: Even accomplished skiers may take a long look before deciding whether today’s the day.

In a recent development, not every intimidating entrance involves a giant cliff or mandatory air. Sometimes it’s what you can’t see that gets the adrenaline going. Lobotomy, located off of Silver King peak, in Crystal’s sidecounty zone, is known for its blind entrance and consequential no-fall-zone skiing. You can’t simply peer over the edge and map out every turn before committing. It’s a different kind of mental challenge, and one that earns this line a spot on the list. Note that this is technically hike-to terrain, so come prepared with all the necessary equipment.

Snowbird is for its steep skiing, and Pipeline Couloir is one of its more intimidating challenges. Getting there requires a hike, but the real test begins when skiers reach the entrance: a steep, rocky drop-in that demands solid technical skills before the couloir even opens up. It’s a reminder that sometimes the most intimidating part of a substantial-mountain line isn’t the descent itself, but getting those first few turns just right.

Industry observers note that revelstoke is a playground for skiers who like their terrain steep, deep, and a little intimidating. With a technical entrance and steep, demanding terrain, Discipline rewards, well, discipline and confident, precise skiing. Depending on conditions, the entrance can feature a cornice that adds another layer of commitment.

The East Coast gets in on the fun with this Mad River Glen adventure. Paradise is an all-natural trail that starts with a steep drop-in before winding through tight trees, bumps, and rugged New England terrain. There’s no wide-open groomed runway here, and the entrance sets the tone for all that follows. Paradise offers a totally different vibe than all the others on this list, but it’s no less intimidating for those who dare.
